title: The Hermit Tarot Card Meaning: Upright, Reversed & Love
description: The Hermit upright: solitude, reflection, inner guidance; reversed: isolation or no quiet. Love, work, advice and Waite's 1911 text. Ask your question.
image_alt: The Hermit, 1909 Rider–Waite–Smith card: a gray-bearded old man in a long gray hooded cloak holds up a glowing lantern and leans on a tall yellow staff, standing on a white peak.
capsule: The Hermit is card IX of the Major Arcana: solitude, reflection and the wisdom you find once the noise drops away. Reversed, quiet becomes isolation, or busyness crowds it out. It is a calm card asking for time, not a lonely one. On a yes-or-no question it is not clear yet; his light reaches only a few steps ahead.

blocks.heading: What is on The Hermit card?
paragraphs: An old man with a long gray beard stands alone on a white, jagged peak, wrapped in a gray hooded cloak that reaches the ground. He holds a lantern up in his right hand and grips a tall yellow staff with his left, eyes lowered. Waite writes that "it is a star which shines in the lantern" and that the figure is "holding up his beacon on an eminence" (p. 104).
His robed figure fills almost the whole height of the 1909 card. The lantern gives a yellow glow with short rays around it, the sky behind him is a pale blue-gray, and IX appears above his hood.

His beacon, Waite says, intimates "where I am, you also may be" (p. 104). Earlier in the book he calls this "a card of attainment" rather than "a card of quest" (p. 17), and lists older names for the figure: the Capuchin and, in more philosophical language, the Sage (p. 16).

blocks.heading: What did Waite write about The Hermit?
paragraphs: Waite's upright list opens with prudence and circumspection, good judgment and care, then turns to several kinds of deceit. The reversed list is about hiding and holding back: concealment, disguise, fear, caution with no good reason behind it.

In his own reading the lamp counts for more than the hiding. He saw a counsel of prudence in the Hermit "pursuing a solitary path by the light of his own lamp" (p. 22), and he rejected linking the card with "occult isolation", a closed-off kind of self-protection (p. 104).

blocks.heading: What does The Hermit mean upright?
paragraphs: Upright, The Hermit points to solitude chosen on purpose: stepping back from the noise so you can hear your own answers. The card turns up when outside advice has stopped helping and you need time to think before you choose.
The lantern is the heart of it. It shows only the ground just ahead, and that is enough to walk by. Reflection here is practical: one question held long enough for inner guidance to come through.

Wisdom in this card is earned slowly and shared quietly. Time alone with yourself is not loneliness here but focus. If this fits your situation, one question to carry is: what do I need some quiet to hear clearly?

blocks.heading: What does The Hermit mean reversed?
paragraphs: Reversed, The Hermit can point to isolation that has stopped helping: a withdrawal that began as rest and turned into a wall. Or the opposite, constant busyness, avoiding quiet so that reflection never gets a turn.
Waite's reversed words, concealment, disguise and fear, sit near the first reading: pulling back and keeping hidden. The second, a life too full for silence, is a modern reading, not Waite's.
Both leave you without a clear inner signal. Ask whether you need more quiet or more company right now, and give yourself a little of whichever is missing.

blocks.heading: What does The Hermit mean in love?
paragraphs: In love, The Hermit puts understanding your own heart before sharing it. Unpartnered, you may be drawn to time spent getting to know yourself, so that what you look for in someone comes from a clearer place.

Inside a relationship, it can ask for room to think: a quiet evening, a walk alone, space to sort out what you feel before you talk it over. Needing space is not the same as pulling away, and the card speaks only of your side.

Reversed in love, notice whether solitude has become a hiding place, or whether you stay so busy with others that you never check in with yourself. What do you know about your own wishes that you have not said aloud?

blocks.heading: What does The Hermit mean for work and money?
paragraphs: At work, The Hermit favors deep, focused work and time to think things through: research, study, a plan made slowly. It may also suggest looking for a mentor with more experience, or to becoming that guide for someone else.
Where money is concerned, notice how you decide: do you give yourself room to think, or let noise and comparison push you along?
Reversed, check whether you have cut yourself off from people who could help, or are too busy to step back and see the whole picture.

blocks.heading: What is The Hermit's advice?
paragraphs: Take a walk alone and carry one open question with you, without rushing to answer it. The Hermit's advice is to protect a small pocket of quiet in your day and listen to whatever surfaces there.

blocks.heading: Is The Hermit a yes or no card?
The Hermit as a person and as a feeling
paragraphs: In a spread, The Hermit can stand for a mentor, a quiet thinker, or someone who keeps a little apart and sees clearly because of it. Read as you, it marks the quiet part of yourself that knows more than it says. The mood is calm and inward, sometimes a pull toward being alone; reversed, it slides into loneliness or a restlessness that cannot sit still.

pairs.text: Inner knowing beside reflection. Trust the quiet answer you can already half hear.
Retreat twice over. Real rest is the task, not a delay.
Stillness, then movement. Let the time apart set a direction before you push forward.
A pause to take stock. Look at what has grown before you decide what to tend next.

blocks.heading: The Hermit or the Eight of Cups?
paragraphs: Both cards show a lone figure apart from others. In the Eight of Cups, "a man of dejected aspect is deserting the cups" of his past efforts (p. 210); the modern reading is walking away to search for meaning. The Hermit is further along: Waite set him on a height with his beacon raised. The Eight is about leaving something behind; The Hermit, about the quiet you find once you stop and look inward.

blocks.heading: Questions to ask yourself about The Hermit
paragraphs: What question keeps coming back when things get quiet?
Where do I need more silence, and where more company?
What do I already know that I have been too busy to hear?

faq.q: Is The Hermit a good or bad card?
faq.a: Neither, really: it is a thoughtful card. It supports rest, stillness and finding answers of your own, and it cautions only against staying withdrawn after the quiet has done its work. With lively or social cards nearby, it may simply ask for a little time to yourself.

faq.q: Does The Hermit mean being lonely?
faq.a: No. It describes solitude you choose, not loneliness forced on you. Waite saw the figure as someone who has already reached a height and raises a light others can follow. If loneliness is what you feel, the reversed side comes closer: a silence that has lasted longer than it helps.

faq.q: What is inside The Hermit's lantern?
faq.a: A star, in Waite's words (p. 104). His only change to the older design concerned the light: "the lamp is not enveloped partially in the mantle of its bearer" (p. 104). Earlier commentators said the lantern held "the Light of Occult Science" (p. 17), a reading Waite felt missed the higher side of the card.

faq.q: Does The Hermit tell me to cut people off?
faq.a: Not as a rule. Its quiet is meant to send you back with something clearer to share, and the reversed side already marks a retreat that has gone on too long. Stepping back for a while and closing a door for good are different choices; the card asks only for the first.

waite.quote: Prudence, circumspection; also and especially treason, dissimulation, roguery, corruption. Reversed: Concealment, disguise, policy, fear, unreasoned caution.
